title: Kolkata police raid markets as Bengal orders crackdown on hoarding of oil, sugar and potatoes
dek: Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari told officials to act against traders creating artificial shortages, after mustard oil rose to more than ₹210 a litre.
body:
Teams from the Kolkata Police's Enforcement Branch inspected wholesale and retail markets across the city on Wednesday, a day after Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari ordered police and district officials to take "stringent action" against traders accused of hoarding essential goods and holding back supplies to push up prices.

Officers visited Koley Market near Sealdah, Lake Market, Shyambazar, College Street and BB Ganguly Street, checking prices, stock levels and the gap between wholesale and retail rates, and looking for signs of hoarding or artificial shortages, according to reports. No seizures or arrests had been reported by Wednesday evening.

## What the chief minister ordered

Mr Adhikari chaired a meeting at Nabanna, the state secretariat, on Tuesday with senior officials, officials of the Agriculture Marketing Department and representatives of traders' associations. He expressed concern at what officials described as an abnormal rise in the prices of mustard oil, sugar and potatoes, and asked for explanations for the increases in oil and sugar, reports said.

According to reports of the meeting, he directed officials to:

- act promptly against traders and middlemen who withhold stock or restrict supply to create shortages;
- investigate whether shortages were being created artificially;
- buy produce directly from farmers and producers where possible, cutting out intermediaries;
- hold regular meetings with trade associations every Monday to review the market; and
- coordinate closely with Agriculture Marketing Department officials in every district.

He also questioned the Enforcement Branch's role in controlling prices and said it must become more proactive, reports said. One report said he warned that strict action would follow if prices were not brought under control within three days. Traders' associations were asked to report any wholesaler or retailer deliberately cutting supplies.

## How much prices have risen

The state government has not published price figures, and reports differ. Mustard oil, a staple in Bengali kitchens, was selling at ₹210 to ₹230 a litre in Kolkata's retail markets, up from about ₹150, according to one report; another put it at more than ₹220, against about ₹170 a week earlier. Retail sugar was reported at ₹68 to ₹70 a kilo, up from about ₹55 during Durga Puja, while wholesale sugar was reported at about ₹65 a kilo, from ₹50 to ₹55. Potatoes and many vegetables were also selling at "considerably high prices", reports said, without giving figures.

Officials have linked the vegetable price rise to the prolonged rain brought by Cyclone Akvan earlier this month, which damaged winter crops and disrupted supplies to city markets. The state has announced ₹205 crore in relief for farmers whose crops were damaged.

## Why it matters

Food prices are a sensitive issue for any Bengal government, and the crackdown is one of the first big tests on the cost of living for the BJP government that took office in the state this year. Potatoes are especially sensitive: Bengal is one of India's largest potato producers, and potato prices have long been a political issue in the state.

The opposition Trinamool Congress had not issued a formal response to the crackdown by Wednesday evening.

## What happens next

Departments have been told to hold separate meetings with traders' associations as soon as possible to work out measures to stabilise prices, followed by the weekly Monday reviews. The chief minister has also ordered regular joint inspections by the police and the agriculture marketing department across the state, one report said, so further market checks are expected outside Kolkata.
